content: 1. Research should focus on understanding the individual-level impacts and behavioral changes that occur after HIV testing among adolescents, regardless of their HIV status. 2. It is essential to investigate interventions that effectively promote HIV Testing and Counseling (HTC) among adolescent members of key populations. 3. Studies are needed in countries where the age of consent for HIV testing has been lowered to ensure that this policy change has not resulted in riskier behaviors among young people. Existing evidence from sex education programs, which demonstrate no increase in risky behaviors, can serve as a framework for this research. 4. Determining the number of individuals who need to be tested and linked to care, including antenatal care (ANC), as well as linked to prevention interventions such as circumcision, contraception, and preventive behavioral strategies, is critical. 5. Cost-effectiveness data must be collected to evaluate the financial feasibility of these interventions. 6. The cost per person identified as HIV-positive and subsequently linked to prevention and care services should be assessed using various approaches. 7. Research should address the magnitude of attrition and the reasons for it at each step of the HIV treatment cascade. 8. Rigorous evaluation of interventions designed to link adolescents to HIV care and retain them in care is necessary. 9. Interventions should also focus on linking and retaining young people from key populations in HIV care. 10. Gender-related barriers to retention in HIV care must be identified and addressed. 11. The integration of HIV care into school-based settings should be explored for feasibility, cost-effectiveness, and outcomes. 12. Decentralization of HIV care services should be evaluated for its feasibility, cost-effectiveness, and clinical outcomes, particularly in the adolescent age group. 13. Optimal strategies for pre-ART (antiretroviral therapy) retention should be identified through systematic reviews of existing models of pre-ART care for adolescents. 14. Integration of HIV care with sexual and reproductive health (SRH) services for youth presenting with sexually transmitted infections (STIs) or other indicators of unsafe sexual practices should be prioritized. 15. Interventions should be developed to support parents and guardians in facilitating disclosure of HIV status to adolescents. 16. Supportive interventions should also help adolescents make informed decisions about beneficial disclosure of their HIV status. 17. Training programs for healthcare providers should be implemented to improve their ability to support adolescents in HIV care. 18. Effective interventions for sustained adherence to antiretroviral therapy (ART) among adolescents should be identified and implemented. 19. Psychosocial and economic factors, as well as treatment literacy, should be considered when designing community-based initiatives, as not all such initiatives are effective. 20. Clinical outcomes and patient preferences, particularly among adolescents, should guide the decentralization of HIV care services. Data suggest that retention in care may improve with decentralization. 21. Shortand long-term psychosocial outcomes for adolescents living with HIV should be evaluated to ensure comprehensive care. 22. The inability to disclose HIV status at home or in social settings may contribute to gender disparities in ART adherence and retention in care. 23. Social support and disclosure of HIV status are predictors of mental health outcomes in HIV-positive youth. 24. Interventions should address the unique challenges faced by adolescents in accessing and adhering to HIV care, including stigma, gender dynamics, and socioeconomic barriers. 25. The integration of HIV testing into routine healthcare visits, such as immunization clinics, has been shown to increase the identification of HIV-positive individuals and should be further explored. 26. Comprehensive sexuality education, when evidence-informed, does not lead to increased risky behaviors and should be promoted as part of HIV prevention strategies. 27. The role of family and social relationships in supporting adolescents living with HIV should be emphasized, as these factors significantly impact psychological well-being and adherence to treatment. 28. Research should continue to explore the predictors and outcomes of HIV status disclosure among adolescents, as disclosure is associated with improved clinical and psychosocial outcomes. 29. Gender-specific barriers to HIV care, such as the inability to take medications openly at home, should be addressed to improve adherence and retention in care. 30. The integration of HIV care with maternal and child health services, including prevention of mother-to-child transmission (PMTCT) programs, should be optimized to improve outcomes for both mothers and children. 31. Interventions should address the unique needs of adolescents living with HIV, including mental health support, treatment literacy, and strategies to reduce stigma and discrimination. 32. The development of evidence-based policies and programs for adolescents living with HIV should be informed by rigorous research and systematic reviews of existing interventions.
